rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - one-season (2024-25) RBD field experiment on 4-year-old guava, Baruipur, West Bengal, eight treatments (four irrigation methods with/without capacitive soil moisture sensor), three replications. Q2: Table 1 and Table 2 / Results - SMS reduced seasonal irrigated water in every method (e.g. flood 17965 vs 11396 l/plot; drip 9060 vs 3337 l/plot), raised irrigation efficiency (drip+SMS 89.94% vs flood no-SMS 25.10%) and saved 28-63% water. Q9: Tables 1 and 2 report SEM and CD(0.05) for water irrigated per plot and for conveyance, field application and irrigation efficiency.
rows.notes: Single method (plot water accounting and efficiency calculation), one site, one crop, one season, 20 m2 plots. Irrigation interval and frequency are reported (Table 1, Fig. 1) but no soil-moisture readings or other intermediate variable are presented, so Q4 kept at no. No limitations stated. Water-saving percentage column itself lacks SEM, but the underlying water and efficiency values have SEM. Abstract and text contain inconsistent figures (5.53 vs 553 times; 3.51 vs 1.027).

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods - own field experiment on guava with soil moisture sensors under four irrigation methods.
rows.notes: The study tests a capacitive soil moisture sensor read manually, with irrigation applied by hand on the basis of sensor readings; there is no app, IoT architecture, automation or scheduling software, and no measurement of operational delays. It shows SMS-guided manual irrigation reduced water use and raised irrigation efficiency, which is evidence about soil sensors, not app-based scheduling.
